clue.text: The light and yielding Iris

definitions.note: the definition stands for the sign of yielding, a symbol of surrender rather than an adjective

parts.note: light in colour, pale, as white is
the flag is the common name of the iris plant

explanation.surface: A pale iris flower somehow carries a meaning of giving way.
explanation.walkthrough: A white iris is a white flag in gardener's terms, and the white flag is what a side waves when it surrenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving a pale banner is the traditional signal of surrender in war.

clue.text: Composer a spider made turn about

parts.note: what a spider spins and makes is a web

indicators.note: turn tells us to turn the next word round so it reads backwards

parts.note: about means concerning, re

explanation.surface: A composer watches a spider spin and then spin round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' acts on RE (from 'about'), giving ER after WEB. Carl Maria von Weber was a German Romantic composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Maria von Weber wrote the opera Der Freischütz, so he is a composer.

clue.text: Whose territory one ship circumnavigates

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: sailing right round something puts the ship's letters around the other piece

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
territory is land

explanation.surface: A riddle about places a single ship can sail all the way around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circumnavigates' puts SS (steamship) round LAND, after I for 'one'; the whole clue also describes the answer, since a ship can sail round an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Pieces of land surrounded by sea are the territory a ship may sail completely around.

clue.text: The mundane Turner

parts.note: mundane is read as earthly, and a Turner as something that turns over the soil, not the painter

explanation.surface: An ordinary, unexciting J.M.W. Turner, the painter, brought down to earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner looks like the English painter; here it means a creature that turns the soil, and 'mundane' is used in its root sense of 'of the earth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Worms burrow through and turn over garden soil, so they are earthly turners.

clue.text: A famous singer is a long way to the 21 east of the island

parts.note: Jenny Lind, the Swedish Nightingale, was a famous soprano
a long way off is far
21-down is the compass point north, and north-east is abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: A celebrated singer is said to live far off, towards the north-east of an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The '21' refers to the answer of 21-down, NORTH, so '21 east' means north-east, NE. Lindisfarne, or Holy Island, lies off the Northumberland coast in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Lindisfarne is a tidal islet off England's north-east coast, also called Holy Island.

clue.text: Pain, of a college servant

explanation.surface: Discomfort suffered by a university servant.
explanation.walkthrough: A gyp is a college servant at Cambridge, and 'to give someone gyp' is British slang for causing pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Gyp is British slang for pain or trouble, and also the name for a manservant at Cambridge colleges.

clue.text: Is angry at atmospheric pollution

explanation.surface: Someone is furious about dirty air.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who seethes with rage is angry; smoke and exhaust gases are the pollution of the air.

clue.text: The expressman was Thursday's child perhaps

definitions.text: The expressman was Thursday's child perhaps

parts.words: The expressman was Thursday's child perhaps
parts.note: the nursery rhyme says Thursday's child has far to go, and the express company founder's surname splits that way

explanation.surface: Was the founder of a delivery firm born on a Thursday?
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme 'Monday's child', Thursday's child has 'far to go'. William Fargo co-founded the Wells Fargo express company, and his name splits as FAR GO.
explanation.definitionFit: William Fargo was a founder of the American Express and Wells Fargo carrier companies.

clue.text: Whom puss catches catches me with a Japanese waitress

indicators.note: the second catches says the first piece holds the next inside it

parts.note: a cat catches a mouse
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cat catches someone in the company of a waitress from Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'catches' looks like a misprint but is needed: the first is part of 'Whom puss catches' (a mouse), the second says MOUSE catches ME inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousmee is an old borrowing from Japanese musume, a girl, used for a young waitress or teahouse girl.

clue.text: A noted outsider

parts.note: noted is read as making musical notes, and outsider as one who stands outside a window to sing

explanation.surface: A well-known person who does not belong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like 'famous'; it means 'producing notes', and the outsider is someone singing beneath a beloved's window at night.
explanation.definitionFit: A singer who performs love songs outdoors beneath a window is making music outside.

clue.text: Battle whose issue was a toss up ?

definitions.text: Battle whose issue was a toss up ?

parts.words: Battle whose issue was a toss up ?
parts.note: a toss-up usually means an evenly balanced outcome, but a charging bull's rush ends in tossing someone in the air

explanation.surface: A battle whose result was uncertain, like a coin toss.
explanation.walkthrough: Bull Run was a battle of the American Civil War; a bull's run at someone ends in tossing them up on its horns.
explanation.definitionFit: Two Civil War battles in Virginia, in 1861 and 1862, are named after the creek called Bull Run.

clue.text: The Scottish plaintiff is after you !

explanation.surface: A litigant north of the border is chasing someone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots law the party bringing a civil action is called the pursuer, not the plaintiff.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots law calls the party bringing a civil case by this name; someone chasing you is one who follows behind.

clue.text: Largely the stock situation

parts.note: stock is read as livestock, and the situation as the large place where cattle are kept

explanation.surface: Broadly speaking, how things stand on the stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock situation' suggests finance; here stock is cattle, and the place is a large farm where they are reared.
explanation.definitionFit: A big livestock farm in the American West is where cattle are raised in large numbers.

clue.text: Where legs are arms

parts.note: arms means a coat of arms, and on this island's emblem the device is three running legs

explanation.surface: A strange place where limbs swap roles.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, has a coat of arms showing three armoured legs joined at the thigh, the triskelion.
explanation.definitionFit: The Manx flag and heraldic shield show three legs, so there the legs are the island's arms.

clue.text: They make well-angled scoops

parts.note: well-angled is read as well angled, that is fished well, and scoops as lifting fish from the water

explanation.surface: Things that produce journalistic scoops from cleverly chosen angles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoops' and 'angle' suggest journalism; here an angler scoops a hooked fish out of the water with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglers use long-handled mesh bags to lift a caught fish from the water.

clue.text: Shady character we see taking cover

indicators.note: taking away, so the last word is removed from the first

parts.note: to see or find is to discover
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspicious person spotted diving for cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' here means taking away: remove COVER from DISCOVER (we see) to leave DIS. Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, the realm of the shades, hence 'shady'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dis, the Roman ruler of the dead, reigns over the shades or ghosts of the underworld.

clue.text: It could give the economy a bumpy ride

definitions.text: It could give the economy a bumpy ride

parts.words: It could give the economy a bumpy ride
parts.note: an economic fall in prices is read also as letting the air out of a tyre, which makes for a rough journey

explanation.surface: Something that might shake up the national economy.
explanation.walkthrough: The economic sense is a fall in prices and activity; the other sense is a let-down tyre, which gives a bumpy ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A general fall in prices and money supply is the economic term, while a flat tyre has lost its air.

clue.text: Nutlessly nutty

explanation.surface: Mad, without any nuts at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The nut is slang for the head, so being without one's nut is being off one's head; the phrase also means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Nut is slang for head, so nutless is head-free; nutty and the phrase both mean mad.

clue.text: Help! A number broken out Hold on

parts.note: SOS is the distress call asking for help
ten is a number

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the next word are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A cry for help as a crowd breaks out, telling someone to hang on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges OUT into UTO after SOS and TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical direction tells a player to sustain the notes, keeping them held.

clue.text: Uncaged birds are barren cattle

parts.note: an uncaged bird is free
martins are birds of the swallow family

explanation.surface: Released birds turn out to be sterile cows.
explanation.definitionFit: A freemartin is a sterile female calf born twin to a bull calf, hence barren cattle.

clue.text: Up medico, cry "Take me to your heart "

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the pieces read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: MO is a medical officer
to cry is to sob

explanation.surface: A doctor calls out a plea for affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns the whole run MO + SOB + ME backwards, giving EM BOS OM.
explanation.definitionFit: To clasp someone to your breast is to take them lovingly to your heart.

clue.text: To make things worse have a gin on the side

indicators.note: the answer must have the other word put on it to form the longer word, so that word is taken away

parts.note: the side or edge of a page is the margin
gin as in the drink

explanation.surface: Drinking gin on the side only makes matters worse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'have a gin on' as 'add GIN to': the answer plus GIN gives MARGIN, the side, so remove GIN from MARGIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil or damage something is to make it worse.

clue.text: Wine for winter escapists

parts.note: the name of a fortified wine is also an Atlantic island where people go to escape the northern winter

explanation.surface: A drink for people who dislike the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Madeira is both a fortified wine and a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, popular with Britons fleeing winter.
explanation.definitionFit: The fortified wine is named after the island it comes from, a mild winter resort.

clue.text: Composer who floated to Britain in the Ice Age?

definitions.text: Composer who floated to Britain in the Ice Age?

parts.words: Composer who floated to Britain in the Ice Age?
parts.note: the composer's names suggest an iceberg, which floats, coming to Albion or Alba, an old name for Britain

explanation.surface: A fanciful history of a composer drifting to Britain long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Alban suggests Alba or Albion, old names for Britain, and Berg suggests an iceberg, which floats. Alban Berg was an Austrian composer of the Second Viennese School.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg wrote the operas Wozzeck and Lulu, so he is a composer.

clue.text: Responsibility for the Tea Party in this quarter ?

definitions.text: Responsibility for the Tea Party in this quarter ?

parts.words: Responsibility for the Tea Party in this quarter ?
parts.note: the British prime minister blamed for the Boston Tea Party shares his name with a compass point, a quarter

explanation.surface: Whose fault was a tea party in this part of town?
explanation.walkthrough: Lord North was British prime minister at the time of the Boston Tea Party of 1773; a quarter here is a point of the compass.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the four cardinal points, or quarters, of the compass, as well as the surname of the prime minister Lord North.

clue.text: Defended to the last over

indicators.note: only the final letters of the word are kept, read to its end

explanation.surface: Someone held out until the very end of the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the last' takes the last five letters of 'Defended'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something finished or concluded is over.

clue.text: "Hello" girl bidden "good-bye" in the Boer War

definitions.text: "Hello" girl bidden "good-bye" in the Boer War

parts.words: "Hello" girl bidden "good-bye" in the Boer War
parts.note: a girl greeted in one famous song title and bade farewell in the popular Boer War song Goodbye ... Gray

explanation.surface: A telephone operator said farewell to during the South African war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goodbye Dolly Gray' was a popular song of the Boer War (1899-1902); 'Hello' also suggests the 'hello girl', an old name for a telephone operator.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name greeted in a song title and bidden farewell in a famous wartime song.

clue.text: A stormy sunrise brings business to underwriters

indicators.note: a stormy sea is tossed about, so the letters of the next word are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Bad weather at dawn means more work for the insurance trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stormy' rearranges the letters of SUNRISE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who takes out a policy against risk pays premiums, giving work to the underwriters.

clue.text: It's your turn in France to be short of English money

indicators.note: turn means the French word is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: in France, your (plural, polite) is vos

explanation.surface: In France it is someone's go to be out of pocket in sterling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' says to put 'your' into French, VOS, which 'turn' then reverses. A sov is short for a sovereign, an old English gold coin worth a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: A sov is the shortened name of the sovereign, the English gold pound coin.

clue.text: Of zoological shedding

parts.note: a plain description of an adjective meaning relating to the cast skins or shells animals shed

explanation.surface: A technical term about animals shedding their outer layers.
explanation.definitionFit: Exuviae are the cast skins or shells that animals such as snakes and insects moult.

clue.text: Ophelia in her orisons

parts.note: points to Hamlet's line greeting Ophelia at her prayers, where orisons means prayers

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's tragic heroine at prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, the prince greets Ophelia with 'Nymph, in thy orisons be all my sins remember'd'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet addresses Ophelia at her prayers by this word for a beautiful young maiden.

clue.text: Like Joel's young men and Wordsworth's gleam

definitions.text: Like Joel's young men and Wordsworth's gleam

parts.words: Like Joel's young men and Wordsworth's gleam
parts.note: the prophet Joel says young men shall see visions

explanation.surface: A literary comparison drawing on the Bible and a Romantic poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Joel 2:28 says 'your young men shall see visions'; Wordsworth's Immortality Ode asks 'Whither is fled the visionary gleam?'
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sees visions, or a light seen in a dream, is prophetic and imaginative.
